lesson.title: Building a Formula Out of Balanced Charge
lesson.summary: Ionic compounds are electrically neutral solids built from repeating ratios of cations and anions, and their formulas, properties, and behavior all trace back to the strength of the electrostatic attraction holding those ions together.
lesson.body:
An ionic compound is what results when the ionic bonding covered previously plays out across a full sample of matter rather than just a single pair of ions. Because opposite charges attract in every direction, not just along one line between two specific ions, a single Na+ ion does not pair off with just one Cl- ion the way two atoms share a single covalent bond, instead, each ion is surrounded by multiple ions of the opposite charge, and the entire solid becomes one continuous, electrically balanced structure. The formula written for an ionic compound, like NaCl, is therefore not a description of an individual molecule the way a covalent formula like H2O is, it is a formula unit, representing the simplest whole number ratio of cations to anions needed to keep the overall compound electrically neutral.

That neutrality requirement is what actually determines an ionic compound's formula, and it follows directly from the charges the ions carry once electrons are transferred. Sodium loses one electron to form Na+ and chlorine gains one electron to form Cl-, so a one to one ratio balances the charge exactly, giving the formula NaCl. Calcium, however, loses two electrons to form Ca2+, so pairing it with chloride, which still only carries a single negative charge as Cl-, requires two chloride ions for every calcium ion to balance the charge, giving the formula CaCl2. This same logic scales to compounds built from ions of any charge: magnesium oxide pairs Mg2+ with O2- in a simple one to one ratio, since the charges already match, giving the formula MgO.

The extended, all directions attraction inside an ionic solid also explains several signature physical properties that set ionic compounds apart from covalently bonded molecular substances. Because every ion is held in place by strong electrostatic attraction to several neighboring ions of the opposite charge at once, ionic compounds tend to have high melting points, sodium chloride does not melt until 801 degrees Celsius. That same rigid, charge balanced arrangement also makes ionic solids brittle rather than malleable: striking an ionic crystal can shift one layer of ions slightly out of alignment with the layer next to it, suddenly lining up ions of the same charge face to face, and the resulting repulsion is often strong enough to shatter the crystal along a clean plane, in sharp contrast to how a metal simply deforms under the same kind of stress.

Ionic compounds also behave very differently depending on their physical state, which is a direct test of whether their ions are free to move. In the solid state, the ions are locked into fixed positions within the crystal and cannot carry a current, so solid ionic compounds do not conduct electricity. Once melted, or once dissolved in water, the ions become free to move independently, and the compound conducts electricity readily, which is exactly why molten salts and salt solutions are used as electrolytes. This solid versus molten or dissolved distinction is one of the most reliable diagnostic tests for identifying an ionic compound in the first place, and it sets up the final piece of this picture: the specific, repeating three dimensional arrangement that ions adopt in the solid state, known as the crystal lattice.
